Here are the verse-by-verse notes for Ephesians 2, drawn from the sources I was able to reach. (Search and fetch limits prevented reading every planned page, but what I did obtain is substantial.)

---

## Ephesians 2 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary

### v. 1

**"And you were dead in your trespasses and sins"**

- The words "He made alive" (KJV "hath he quickened") are not in the Greek but are supplied from v.5 to complete the sense. Paul addresses believers who once were spiritually dead but are now alive through God's work. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-2/ , https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ephesians/2.htm

- "Dead" (*nekros*) refers to a corpse. Paul is saying "You were corpses!" — spiritually separated from God, unable to initiate any movement toward Him. The verb "were" is in a form indicating a continuous state. Every person is born "D.O.A." spiritually because of the sin virus inherited from Adam (Rom. 5:12). — https://www.preceptaustin.org/ephesians_21-2

- Gill notes three dimensions of this death: (a) dead in Adam as federal head, (b) dead in a legal sense under the sentence of condemnation, and (c) dead morally through original sin and actual transgressions — a loss of original righteousness, a deformation of God's image, and a privation of spiritual capacity. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ephesians/2.htm

- Ellicott distinguishes the two Greek words: "trespass" (*paraptōma*) means a swerving aside, a falling — pointing to visible, specific acts of failure. "Sins" (*hamartia*) means a missing of the mark — denoting universal and positive principles of evil-doing. Together they form a climax. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ephesians-2.html

- Enduring Word notes a theological controversy: in what sense is the unregenerate person "dead"? The Bible uses many pictures of the lost condition (blind, enslaved, sick, lost, alien), so "dead in trespasses and sins" does not say everything about man's lost state. It is therefore valid to appeal to all people to believe; we need not look for evidence of regeneration before calling people to faith. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-2/

- The Haydock Catholic Commentary explains: "You were dead to the eyes of God, but you live in the eyes of the world… according to the maxims of the world, in idolatry, in crime, in corruption of manners." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/ephesians/2.htm

### v. 2

**"in which you used to walk when you conformed to the ways of this world and of the ruler of the power of the air, the spirit who is now at work in the sons of disobedience."**

- Precept Austin identifies a "triad of evil" in vv.1–3: the world, the flesh, and the devil — the three ravaging forces that dominated the believer's former life. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/ephesians_21-2

- "Once walked" means the believer's life should now be different. Enduring Word uses the illustration: a dead man feels comfortable in his coffin, but if made alive he would instantly feel suffocated and want to escape. So the regenerate person should feel suffocated by the old life of sin. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-2/

- Ellicott gives a careful analysis: "the course (*age*) of this world" — the transitoriness and unreality of the present life combined with its carnal, material, unspiritual character. "The prince of the power of the air" means "a power dwelling in the region of the air," not power over the air. The air is the cloudy, dark sphere between heaven and earth — a fitting image for the evil power that invisibly encompasses the world yet is overruled by heaven. The word "spirit" is in apposition to "power" (not "prince") — the collective power of evil working in the disobedient is called "a spirit," opposed to the Spirit of God. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ephesians-2.html

- Gill notes it was a common Jewish, Chaldean, Pythagorean, and Platonic belief that the air is full of demons. Satan as Beelzebub is the prince at the head of these, and the demons under him are like flies in the air. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ephesians/2.htm

- Enduring Word adds: the same Greek verb used for Satan's working in unbelievers here (*energeō*) is used in Eph. 3:20 for God's power working in believers — a sobering parallel. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-2/

### v. 3

**"All of us also lived among them at one time, fulfilling the cravings of our flesh and indulging its desires and thoughts. Like the rest, we were by nature children of wrath."**

- Paul now includes himself and other Jews — "we all." This is critical to his argument: Jews and Gentiles were equally dead in sin. The chapter aims to show both groups were in the same desperate condition and are now equally saved by grace. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ephesians/2.htm

- Ellicott: "Flesh" here includes both bodily appetites and the thoughts of the mind; anything in human nature devoted to this visible world and alienated from God. The sins of "the flesh," "the world," and "the devil" are not different classes of sins but different aspects of the same sin. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ephesians-2.html

- "Children of wrath": Ellicott says this is a Hebrew idiom (like "son of death" = one under sentence of death). It means those under God's wrath against sin, not "begotten of wrath" as "children of disobedience" means "begotten of disobedience." The word for "children" (*tekna*) is normally a term of endearment used for relation to God — so its use with "wrath" is startling and paradoxical. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ephesians-2.html

- "By nature": this means what is inborn and common to all, as opposed to what is acquired. The reference is to human nature as alienated from God (not as originally created). "Nature" here is opposed to "grace." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ephesians-2.html

- Enduring Word: The Bible knows nothing of the idea that all people are "children of God" except as common Creator. Here Paul speaks of a "family" of wrath. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-2/

- Gill notes the Jewish commentator Kimchi on Isaiah 43:27: "man is naturally in sin." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ephesians/2.htm

### v. 4

**"But because of His great love for us, God, who is rich in mercy,"**

- The "But God" is one of the great turning points of Scripture. Every reason for God's mercy and love is found in Him, not in us. We were dead, unlovely, children of wrath — yet He loved us. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-2/

- Ellicott: "Rich in mercy" — not merely merciful, but possessing "a multitude of mercy" that reaches even to those dead in sin (citing Chrysostom). The idea of richness in grace, glory, and mercy is characteristic of Ephesians (1:7, 1:18, 2:7, 3:8, 3:16). "Great love" is the one moving cause of salvation (cf. Rom. 5:8). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ephesians-2.html

- Gill: God is "rich" in mercy because He dispenses it freely and liberally to a large number, in great abundance and variety — in the covenant, in Christ's mission, in redemption, in regeneration, in pardon, and in eternal salvation — yet it remains inexhaustible. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ephesians/2.htm

- Clarke (cited by Enduring Word): "As they were corrupt in their nature, and sinful in their practice, they could possess no merit, nor have any claim upon God; and it required much mercy to remove so much misery." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-2/

- Enduring Word: The application is that we must stop trying to make ourselves lovable to God and simply receive His great love while recognizing we are unworthy of it. This is "the grace secret of the Christian life." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-2/

### v. 5

**"made us alive with Christ even when we were dead in our trespasses. It is by grace you have been saved!"**

- God did not wait until we were lovable. He loved us "even when we were dead." This is the requirement for salvation: you must first be dead — dead to every attempt to justify yourself. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-2/

- "Made us alive together with Christ" (*syzōopoieō*): Gill explains this may be understood as regeneration (the infusion of spiritual life where there was death) or justification (when Christ rose, believers rose with Him; when He was justified, they were justified in Him). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ephesians/2.htm

- "By grace you have been saved" is parenthetical — Paul cannot mention this work without reminding us it is entirely of grace, given to the undeserving. Ellicott notes the Greek means "ye have been saved" — a completed act, like justification, but "salvation" also implies a continuous state lasting until the final judgment. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ephesians-2.html

- Enduring Word: This anticipates vv.8–9. Even faith is not the saviour — grace through faith means grace is the water and faith is the hose. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-2/

### v. 6

**"And God raised us up with Christ and seated us with Him in the heavenly realms in Christ Jesus,"**

- This is the present position of the Christian. We are not those who "dwell on the earth" (as Revelation terms the unbelieving) — our citizenship is in heaven (Phil. 3:20). We sit in heavenly places *in* Christ Jesus, not yet *with* Him physically; since our life and identity is in Christ, where He sits, we sit. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-2/

- Ellicott: This is a partaking not only of Christ's resurrection (as in Rom. 6:5) but also of His ascension — a thought peculiar to Ephesians and Colossians. It implies present blessing (by His indwelling through the Spirit) and future fulness. The one thing Paul does *not* attribute to us is "the place at the right hand of the Father" — that belongs to Christ alone. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ephesians-2.html

- Gill: "Made us sit together" speaks of honour, pleasure, rest from labour, and safety. It is spoken of as already accomplished because of its certainty, because of the believer's right to it in Christ, and because Christ the Head already sits there representing His people. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ephesians/2.htm

- Clarke (Enduring Word): "We have a right to the kingdom of God, anticipate this glory, and are indescribably happy in the possession of this salvation, and in our fellowship with Christ Jesus." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-2/

### v. 7

**"in order that in the coming ages He might display the surpassing riches of His grace, demonstrated by His kindness to us in Christ Jesus."**

- God's purpose in saving us is to display His grace — not only now but throughout eternity. God will never stop dealing with believers on the basis of grace. The Church becomes God's exhibit to the universe. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-2/

- Spurgeon (cited by Enduring Word): "When all the saints shall be gathered home they shall still talk and speak of the wonders of Jehovah's love in Christ Jesus, and in the golden streets they shall stand up and tell what the Lord has done for them to listening crowds of angels, and principalities, and powers." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-2/

- Ellicott: "The ages which are coming on" — both ages of time and eternity looked upon in one great continuity. "Kindness" (*chrēstotēs*) means facility or readiness to serve another — God's gentle patience and readiness to receive sinners. It was so marked in Christ's ministry that the Pharisees thought it an over-facility condoning sin. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ephesians-2.html

- Precept Austin's summary: Ephesians 2:1–3 = Amazing Depths; 2:4–7 = Amazing Heights; 2:8–9 = Amazing Grace; 2:10 = Amazing Work. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/ephesians_21-2

### vv. 8–9

**"For it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not by works, so that no one can boast."**

This is one of the most discussed passages in all of Scripture.

- Grace is the moving cause; faith is only the instrument. "Through faith" — Ellicott says this is theologically exact. Grace saves; faith is the channel, not the cause. Lloyd-Jones (Monergism): "Faith is not the cause of salvation. Christ is the cause of salvation… Faith is but the instrument through which it comes to me." — https://www.monergism.com/grace-through-faith-ephesians-28%E2%80%939 , https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ephesians-2.html

- **What does "this" (*touto*) refer to?** This is the key grammatical debate:
  - **Traditional Reformed/Modern view:** "This" (neuter) refers to the whole concept of "salvation by grace through faith," not to "faith" (feminine noun). Calvin adopted this, followed by the great majority of modern commentators. Enduring Word cites Clarke and Alford supporting this reading. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-2/
  - **Ancient Greek-speaking view:** The Gospel Coalition Australia notes that Chrysostom, Jerome, Augustine, Theodoret, Fulgentius, Œcumenius, and Theophylact all took "this" as referring to "faith" — that faith itself is the gift of God. These were native Greek speakers (or had undoubted Greek ability). Their exegetical decision was generally *in spite of* their theological leanings (they tended toward free-will views). — https://au.thegospelcoalition.org.au/article/is-faith-the-gift-of-god-reading-ephesians-28-10-with-the-ancients/
  - Enduring Word straddles: grammatically "this" refers to salvation, but "even our faith is a gift of God. We cannot believe in Jesus unless God does a prior work in us." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-2/

- **"Not of works, lest anyone should boast":** Ellicott notes this sums up the whole argument of Romans 3:27–4:25. Salvation is structured so that God alone receives the glory. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ephesians-2.html

- **Catholic reading:** Catholic Answers notes that the salvation Paul discusses here is *initial* salvation — the kind received at first coming to God and being justified. Catholicism affirms that salvation also has present and future aspects (cf. Phil. 2:12, 1 Pet. 1:8–9), and works done in grace are not excluded from the full picture. — https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/faith-and-works-%200

- **Haydock Catholic Commentary:** "Faith is the beginning, foundation, and the root of justification, and the first of all other virtues, without which it is impossible to please God. Not of works, as of our own growth, or from ourselves: but as from the grace of God." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/ephesians/2.htm

**Denominational differences on grace and faith (vv. 8–9):**

A comparison from the Lutheran Witness (LCMS) lays out the key distinctions:

- **Reformed (bound-will — Christian Reformed, Dutch Reformed):** God's grace is His sovereign election of certain people from before the foundation of the world. Man is entirely deprived of free will. Grace cannot be resisted. Certainty of election comes through the Means of Grace and the Spirit's internal witness. However, they limit Jesus' work of redemption to the elect, so certainty cannot rest simply in the Gospel proclamation. — https://witness.lcms.org/2020/views-on-grace/

- **Reformed/Arminian (free-will — many Baptists, Evangelical Free, Methodists):** Grace is "free in all and free for all" (Wesley). It is not based on works but depends on man's decision to choose Christ; the human will cooperates in conversion. God's grace gives man a free will to make a decision for faith. Certainty rests in the experience of how the human will chooses and responds to the Gospel. — https://witness.lcms.org/2020/views-on-grace/

- **Lutheran:** Grace is God's favor revealed in Christ's redemption by which He declares sinners righteous. It is received fully through faith, which God counts as righteousness. It does not depend at all on human will (Rom. 9:16; Eph. 2:1). The Gospel fully contains and reveals this grace. Certainty is not in an internal witness or human decision but in the objective, complete work of Christ given fully in the Gospel and Sacraments. — https://witness.lcms.org/2020/views-on-grace/

- **Catholic:** Grace involves God's cooperation with man's free will to respond to His call with good works. Faith is the beginning of justification, but salvation encompasses a process. — https://witness.lcms.org/2020/views-on-grace/ , https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/faith-and-works-%200

### v. 10

**"For we are God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus to do good works, which God prepared in advance as our way of life."**

- "Workmanship" translates the Greek *poiēma*, from which we get "poem." We are God's beautiful poem, His work of art. God saves us not merely to rescue us from wrath but to make something beautiful of us. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-2/

- Spurgeon (cited by Enduring Word): "Our new life is as truly created out of nothing as were the first heavens, and the first earth… the grace of God does not improve the old nature into the new. It does nothing of the sort." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-2/

- Good works are not the root from which salvation grows but the fruit God intends it to bear. Paul shows himself at one with James: works play no part in securing salvation, but afterwards Christians prove their faith by their works. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-2/

- Ellicott says this verse contains "perhaps, in all Scripture, no stronger expression of the great mystery of God's predestination" — extending even to the actual good works in which human free-will and energy are most plainly exercised. Yet the paradox is maintained: we "walk" by our own act, and yet God prepared these works beforehand. Both truths — God's preordination and man's responsible freedom — are emphasised; their reconciliation awaits the time when we "know even as we are known." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ephesians-2.html

- Gill: Works cannot be the efficient, moving, or procuring cause of salvation because they are themselves effects — both of the work of grace upon the soul in time (called a "creation") and of the decrees of God from eternity. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ephesians/2.htm

- The Haydock Commentary: "St. Paul now compares our conversion to creation, to show that we had been called and justified without preceding merit. In the same manner as the things which God has drawn out of nothing, cannot glory as if they had contributed any thing to their existence." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/ephesians/2.htm

### vv. 11–12

**"Therefore remember that formerly you who are Gentiles in the flesh and called uncircumcised by the so-called circumcision… remember that at that time you were separate from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers to the covenants of the promise, without hope and without God in the world."**

- Paul now shifts from individual reconciliation to reconciliation between groups — specifically Jew and Gentile. He begins by reminding Gentile believers of their former state. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-2/

- Stott (cited by Enduring Word) summarizes the Gentile condition as "Christless, stateless, friendless, hopeless and Godless." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-2/

- "Without hope": Bruce notes that "the absence of hope in the face of death is amply attested in the literature and epigraphy of the Greco-Roman world." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-2/

- "Without God in the world": even those who believed in a distant deity were functionally godless — God had nothing to do with their world. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-2/

- Alford (Enduring Word) notes that "aliens from the commonwealth of Israel" likely includes lax Jews as well as Gentiles — Israelites outside the commonwealth "not only as foreigners but as lax Jews." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-2/

- Haydock: Gentiles were "without Christ, without the hopes or expectation of the Messias, alienated from the conversation of those who were God's elect people, and from the promises particularly made to them." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/ephesians/2.htm

- Spurgeon (Enduring Word): "Without Christ! If this be the description of some of you, we need not talk to you about the fires of hell; let this be enough to startle you, that you are in such a desperate state as to be without Christ." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-2/

### v. 13

**"But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far away have been brought near through the blood of Christ."**

- "But now" mirrors the "But God" of v.4 — another great turning point. The nearness is only "in Christ Jesus" and only "through the blood of Christ." Gentiles who are not in Christ remain as far off as ever. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-2/

- Enduring Word emphasizes that Paul connects the love of Jesus with His sacrificial death: "Preaching Christ crucified means we preach Jesus full of love — sacrificial, giving, saving love." The only way to be brought near to God is by Christ's blood — not by keeping the law or belonging to a group. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-2/

- Haydock: "By believing in him, you who seemed to be far off, are made near by his blood, by him who died for all." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/ephesians/2.htm

### vv. 14–16

**"For He Himself is our peace, who has made the two one and has torn down the dividing wall of hostility by abolishing in His flesh the law of commandments and decrees. He did this to create in Himself one new man out of the two, thus making peace and reconciling both of them to God in one body through the cross, by which He extinguished their hostility."**

- "He Himself is our peace" — Jesus has not merely made peace; He *is* our peace. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-2/

- "The dividing wall of hostility": Enduring Word explains Jesus broke down the wall between Jew and Gentile by fulfilling the law on our behalf and bearing the penalty for our failure to keep it. This created "one new man" — not an improved Gentile or an improved Jew, but a new, third entity: the Christian, the new creation in Christ. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-2/

- "Abolishing in His flesh the law of commandments and decrees": Ellicott notes this refers to the ceremonial law with its ordinances that created the separation between Jew and Gentile. The moral law is not abolished, but the ceremonial law that stood as a barrier is removed in Christ's flesh. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ephesians-2.html

- Haydock: Christ "hath brought peace to all men, breaking down by his incarnation and death that wall of partition, that enmity betwixt the Jews and Gentiles, making them but one; abolishing that former law, of so many ordinances, precepts, and ceremonies." Haydock notes St. Jerome's reading: "abolishing the old law and its precepts by the precepts and doctrine of the new law." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/ephesians/2.htm

- "One new man": this is the Church — one mystical body of which Christ is the Head, reconciling both to God "through the cross." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/ephesians/2.htm

### vv. 17–18

**"He came and preached peace to you who were far away and peace to those who were near. For through Him we both have access to the Father by one Spirit."**

- "Far away" = Gentiles; "near" = Jews. Christ preached peace to both — though His earthly ministry was primarily to Israel, through the apostles the Gospel went to the Gentiles. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-2/

- "Access to the Father by one Spirit": Gill explains this as the Trinitarian work of salvation — through Christ the Son, to the Father, by the Holy Spirit. Both Jew and Gentile now share the same access; there are not two doors. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ephesians/2.htm

- This verse is the foundation for the doctrine that all believers, regardless of background, have equal and direct access to God — a revolutionary idea in the ancient world where temple courts segregated Gentiles from Jews. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-2/

### vv. 19–22

**"Therefore you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God's household, built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus Himself as the cornerstone. In Him the whole building is fitted together and grows into a holy temple in the Lord. And in Him you too are being built together into a dwelling place for God in His Spirit."**

- The image shifts from body to building, from citizenship to household to temple. Believers are no longer outsiders but full citizens and family members. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-2/

- "Foundation of the apostles and prophets": Enduring Word sees this as the apostles and prophets themselves forming the foundation (with their teaching about Christ), not merely their writings — though the two cannot be separated. Christ is the cornerstone (*akrogōniaios*) — the stone that holds the whole structure together, determining the alignment of every other stone. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-2/

- Haydock raises the Catholic point: the Church is "built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets; why not then upon St. Peter?" — acknowledging the text's implications for debates about papal primacy. Haydock answers by affirming all apostles are foundation stones under Christ, who alone is the chief corner-stone. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/ephesians/2.htm

- "Grows into a holy temple": the Church is not static but living and growing. The temple imagery culminates the chapter: believers individually and corporately are the dwelling place of God by His Spirit — the same presence that once filled the Jerusalem temple now indwells the Church. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-2/

- Ellicott summarises the chapter's structure: vv.1–7 = quickening from death; vv.8–10 = all by free grace through faith; vv.11–13 = Gentiles brought near; vv.14–18 = union with Israel in Christ; vv.19–22 = living stones in the great fabric of His Church. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ephesians-2.html

## Summary of the Chapter's Structure (from the sources)

Precept Austin adapts Kent Hughes's memorable outline:

| Section | Theme |
|---|---|
| Eph. 2:1–3 | Amazing Depths (death in sin) |
| Eph. 2:4–7 | Amazing Heights (made alive, raised, seated with Christ) |
| Eph. 2:8–9 | Amazing Grace (salvation as gift) |
| Eph. 2:10 | Amazing Work (created for good works) |

— https://www.preceptaustin.org/ephesians_21-2

Lehman Strauss (Precept Austin) notes a triad structure: (a) three ravaging forces — world, flesh, devil (vv.1–3); (b) three redeeming facts — mercy, love, grace (vv.4–6); (c) three resulting features — made alive together, raised up together, seated together in heavenly places in Christ. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/ephesians_21-2
